# Sitemap & Images — crystalbasket.store

**Audit date:** 2026-09-15 · **Scope:** live `/sitemap.xml` + `/robots.txt` + `/llms.txt` fetched fresh today, cross-checked against `raw/sitemap.json`, `raw/urls.txt`, and the `links`/`images` arrays in all 46 `raw/parsed/*.json` files; 34 unique image files fetched live (HEAD + full GET) from `/images/**` for byte size, format, and pixel dimensions.
**Site facts used below:** static export (`images.unoptimized: true` in `apps/web/next.config.*`, required — Next's Image optimizer cannot run without a server on GitHub Pages); sitemap generated by `apps/web/src/app/sitemap.ts`; hero/listing banners rendered by `apps/web/src/components/Store/Hero.tsx` and `ListingHero.tsx`; product/lifestyle photography is confirmed AI-generated (Higgsfield, 2026-09-03 per `README.md`).

## Scores

| Area | Score |
|---|---|
| **Sitemap** | **74 / 100** |
| **Images** | **59 / 100** |

## Part 1 — Sitemap

### Sitemap scorecard

| Check | Weight | Result | Points |
|---|---|---|---|
| XML format validity | 15 | Well-formed, correct `urlset` namespace, correct `<?xml?>` declaration | 15.0 |
| Coverage vs. crawled internal links | 25 | 46/46 sitemap URLs match crawled links exactly; 0 missing, 0 orphaned/extra | 25.0 |
| `lastmod` accuracy | 20 | All 46 entries share one build-timestamp value; none reflect real content change dates | 3.0 |
| `priority` / `changefreq` hygiene | 10 | `priority` on all 46 (Google ignores it); `changefreq` correctly not used at all | 6.0 |
| Exclusion correctness (`/wishlist/`) | 15 | Disallowed in `robots.txt` and correctly absent from the sitemap, but the page itself has no `noindex` meta tag as a backstop | 12.0 |
| Size/URL-count headroom | 10 | 46 URLs, 6,503 bytes — far under the 50,000-URL / 50 MB cap | 10.0 |
| Image-sitemap opportunity | 5 | Not implemented; would be a minor nice-to-have, not a gap | 3.0 |
| **Total** | **100** | | **74.0** |

### What's already right

- `curl -s https://crystalbasket.store/sitemap.xml` parses cleanly with `xml.dom.minidom` — no malformed tags, correct `xmlns="http://www.sitemapindex.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9"`-style declaration (namespace is the standard `sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9`).
- `robots.txt` declares `Sitemap: https://crystalbasket.store/sitemap.xml` and the file returns live `HTTP/2 200`, `content-type: application/xml`.
- **Coverage is perfect.** I unioned the `links.internal` arrays across all 46 `raw/parsed/*.json` files (47 unique hrefs, including `/wishlist/`) and diffed against the live sitemap's 46 `<loc>` values: the only href in the crawl that is not in the sitemap is `/wishlist/`, which is the one page deliberately excluded (see below). Zero sitemap URLs are missing from the crawl (no orphans/404s/stale entries).
- `/llms.txt` now exists live (confirmed today, well-formed Markdown with brand facts + all 12 products + intentions) — correctly **not** included in the XML sitemap. `llms.txt` is a plain-text discovery file in the same family as `robots.txt`, not an indexable HTML resource, so it has no `<url>` entry to add; no action needed here.
- `changefreq` is not used anywhere — the team already avoided the more actively-misleading of the two deprecated tags.
- Well within Google's per-file caps: 46 URLs and 6.5 KB vs. the 50,000-URL/50 MB ceiling (or the 1,000-URL `news:` cap, not applicable here).

### Findings, ranked

#### 1. (Medium) `lastmod` is the build timestamp, identical on all 46 URLs, not the real last-significant-change date
- **Evidence:** every `<url>` in the live sitemap carries `<lastmod>2026-09-15T11:34:42.908Z</lastmod>` — one single value, 46/46 times. The source is `apps/web/src/app/sitemap.ts`: `const now = new Date();` is computed once per build and stamped onto every entry, including static pages that haven't changed in weeks (`/faq/`, `/disclaimer/`, `/care/`). By contrast, real content dates differ per file — `git log -1 --date=short -- packages/catalog/content/products/the-alchemist.json` → `2026-09-14`, and the last three commits touching `packages/catalog/content/` are dated 2026-09-14, 2026-09-13, and 2026-09-12, i.e. products genuinely change on different days.
- **Is this harmful?** Not a ranking penalty, but it is a wasted signal. Google's own sitemap guidance says that when `lastmod` doesn't reflect a real, meaningful change, Google will stop trusting `lastmod` for that sitemap altogether — at that point every deploy re-stamping all 46 URLs to "now" trains Google to ignore the field entirely rather than use it to prioritize re-crawls of the pages that actually changed (e.g. a stock-status flip on `/products/the-aurora/`). For a 46-page site this doesn't blow a crawl budget, but it does throw away a legitimate freshness signal for zero benefit — an easy, no-downside fix.
- **Fix:** stamp each route with the true last-change date instead of a single `now`:
  - For catalog-driven routes (`/products/[slug]/`, `/stones/[slug]/`, `/intentions/[slug]/`), use the content file's own git history: `git log -1 --format=%aI -- packages/catalog/content/products/<slug>.json` (Node: `execSync` inside `sitemap.ts`, or precompute at build and read a small JSON map).
  - For fully static pages (`/about/`, `/care/`, `/faq/`, `/disclaimer/`, `/size-guide/`), use the git date of the page's copy source (`page.tsx` or wherever the copy lives).
  - **Watch for this gotcha:** `.github/workflows/deploy.yml` uses `actions/checkout@v4` with no `fetch-depth`, which defaults to a **shallow clone (depth 1)** — `git log` on individual files will fail or return only the merge commit inside CI. Add `fetch-depth: 0` to the checkout step before wiring up git-based lastmod, or the dates will silently be wrong again in production even though they look right locally.

#### 2. (Low) `priority` is set on all 46 URLs; Google has ignored this tag since 2009
- **Evidence:** every `<url>` carries a `<priority>` value (1 down to 0.1, reasonably ranked internally: home 1 → shop 0.9 → stacks 0.8 → products 0.8 → intentions 0.7 → stones 0.5 → about/size-guide 0.4 → care/faq 0.3 → disclaimer 0.1).
- **Why it matters:** Google's documentation confirms `priority` is disregarded; Bing does not meaningfully use it either. It isn't harmful, just dead weight in the file (46 extra tags, ~700 bytes).
- **Fix:** optional cleanup — drop the `priority` field from the `sitemap()` return objects in `apps/web/src/app/sitemap.ts`. Not urgent; do it opportunistically the next time that file is touched for the `lastmod` fix above.

#### 3. (Low) `/wishlist/` is excluded via `robots.txt` Disallow only, with no `noindex` backstop on the page itself
- **Evidence:** live `robots.txt` — `Disallow: /wishlist/` (present in both the `User-Agent: *` block and, implicitly, not re-allowed for the AI-crawler group). Live `curl -s https://crystalbasket.store/wishlist/` returns `HTTP/2 200` and `<title>Wishlist · Crystal Basket</title>` with **no** `<meta name="robots">` tag in the HTML. The page is correctly absent from `sitemap.xml`, and it's correctly absent from every other page's crawled internal-link set as a target Google would find by itself, other than the header/footer nav link every page carries.
- **Why it matters:** `robots.txt` Disallow prevents *crawling*, but Google can still index a bare URL (with no snippet) if it discovers the link from crawlable pages — which it will, since every page links to `/wishlist/` in the header. This is the classic "indexed, though blocked by robots.txt" state in Search Console. Low risk here because the page is a client-side, `localStorage`-backed personalization view with no unique server content and unlikely external backlinks, but it's the weaker of the two standard exclusion patterns.
- **Fix:** add `<meta name="robots" content="noindex,follow">` to `apps/web/src/app/wishlist/page.tsx` in addition to (not instead of) the existing `robots.txt` Disallow — belt-and-suspenders is the documented best practice for exactly this case.

#### 4. (Info) An image sitemap would be a minor nice-to-have, not a fix
- **Evidence:** all 34 unique product/lifestyle/hero images are plain, same-origin `<img src="/images/...">` tags embedded directly in server-rendered HTML (confirmed static export, no JS-only injection, no separate image CDN/subdomain) on pages that are already 100% covered by the existing sitemap. Googlebot fully renders and indexes these without any extra help.
- **Why it matters:** Per Google's own guidance, a dedicated `<image:image>` sitemap extension mainly helps when images are hard to discover (JS-rendered, on a different domain, or not otherwise linked from crawlable pages) — none of which applies here. The upside would be marginal: faster initial discovery of new product photos and an explicit canonical-image signal per URL.
- **Fix (optional, low priority):** if/when the catalog grows past ~30-40 more products or moves images to a separate asset host, add `<image:image><image:loc>` entries to the existing `sitemap.ts` output (Next's `MetadataRoute.Sitemap` type supports an `images` array natively) rather than standing up a second sitemap file.

## Part 2 — Images

### Image audit summary

|---|---|

| Missing/empty `alt` (tag instances) | 25 |

| `loading="eager"` / no attribute (above-fold) | 48 |

### Images scorecard

| Category | Weight | Result | Points |
|---|---|---|---|
| Alt text coverage & quality | 25 | Descriptive, non-stuffed text on most product/hub images, but 25 blank instances incl. every hero/listing banner sitewide | 16.25 |

| CLS prevention | 15 | No explicit `width`/`height` anywhere, but every instance checked sits in a fixed-`aspect-ratio` CSS container | 10.5 |

| Modern format adoption (WebP/AVIF) | 15 | 0% adoption; real, quantifiable savings available even under `images.unoptimized` | 5.25 |
| File-size discipline | 10 | Product photos mostly within target tiers; several lifestyle/intention/stack photos in the 200–370 KB warning band | 7.5 |

| **Total** | **100** | | **58.75 → 59** |

### What's already right

- The shared `Img` component (`apps/web/src/components/Img.tsx`) types `alt` as a **required** prop and defaults `loading="lazy"` + `decoding="async"` — a good guardrail that keeps most product-card and content images correctly lazy-loaded with async decoding by default.
- The genuine LCP element (home hero, `hero-1.jpg`) is handled exactly right: `loading` is *not* set (so it defaults to eager) and `fetchPriority="high"` is present — this matches best practice precisely and should not be touched.
- Featured-product images (`the-fortune/main.jpg`, `the-seven/main.jpg`, etc.) below the hero correctly carry `loading="lazy"` in the sample checked.
- Descriptive, hyphenated, keyword-relevant file naming and folder structure throughout: `/images/products/the-alchemist/main.jpg`, `/images/intentions/calm.jpg`, `/images/stacks/protection-stack.jpg` — good for filename-level image SEO, no `IMG_1234.jpg`-style names anywhere.
- Where alt text *is* set, it's genuinely descriptive and not keyword-stuffed: `"The Alchemist — Abundance Bracelet · Citrine & Pyrite"`, `"The Fortune, bead detail"`, `"Stringing gemstone beads at the studio table"`.
- CLS is *functionally* controlled: every image use I traced sits inside a Tailwind `aspect-square` / `aspect-[3/4]` / `aspect-[4/3]` / `aspect-[4/5]` wrapper `<div>`, or (for the two hero components) a section with a fixed `h-[72vh]`/`min-h-[380px]`, so layout space is reserved by CSS even without HTML `width`/`height` attributes.

### Findings, ranked

#### 1. (High) Every hero/listing banner photo sitewide has hardcoded `alt=""` — a single-component bug affecting ~13 pages
- **Evidence:** `apps/web/src/components/Store/Hero.tsx`: `<img src={asset(image)} alt="" className="..." fetchPriority="high" />` — `alt` is hardcoded to an empty string with no prop to override it. `apps/web/src/components/Store/ListingHero.tsx`: `<img src={asset(image)} alt="" className="..." />` — same pattern, also hardcoded. Confirmed live: `home.json` → `hero-1.jpg` alt `""`; `shop.json` → `hero-2.jpg` alt `""`; `intentions.json` → `calm.jpg` (used as the `/intentions/` hub banner) alt `""`; and all 8 individual intention detail pages (`intentions__abundance.json`, `intentions__calm.json`, `intentions__confidence.json`, `intentions__focus.json`, `intentions__grounding.json`, `intentions__love.json`, `intentions__protection.json`, `intentions__sleep.json`) render their own hero photo via the same component with `alt=""`; plus `stones.json` (`/stones/` hub → `studio.jpg`) and `stacks.json` (`stacks-wrist.jpg`). That's 13 page-level banner photos with zero alt text, all traceable to two shared components.
- **Note the inconsistency this creates:** the *same* file `calm.jpg` has real alt text (`"Calm & Ease bracelets"` / `"Calm & Ease on the wrist"`) when it appears as a small tile on the homepage/`/intentions/` grid, but empty alt when the identical file is the full-width banner on `/intentions/calm/`. Same for `studio.jpg` (real alt on `/about/`, empty on `/stones/`).
- **Why it matters:** these are large, prominent, often above-the-fold photographs of the product category (bracelets/stones on a wrist) — exactly the kind of image that can pick up Google Images traffic for queries like "crystal bracelet Dubai" or "protection bracelet". Zero alt text forfeits that opportunity on the site's biggest, most visually prominent images, and undermines the credibility of the good alt text the same files carry elsewhere.
- **Fix:** add an optional `alt` prop to both `Hero` and `ListingHero` (default to the `title` string if not supplied, since that's already passed at every call site) and stop hardcoding `alt=""`. This is a two-line change per component, and every call site already has a natural string to hand it (`title`, or a slightly richer variant like `` `${title} bracelets` ``).

#### 2. (High) `/stacks/` builder grid renders all 12 product photos with `alt=""`
- **Evidence:** `apps/web/src/components/Store/StackBuilder.tsx:38` — `<img src={p.image} alt="" className="h-full w-full object-cover" loading="lazy" />`. Confirmed live in `stacks.json`: every one of the 12 catalog products' `main.jpg` (the-alchemist, the-anchor, the-aurora, the-clear-sight, the-devotion, the-fortune, the-guardian, the-lionheart, the-seven, the-shield, the-still-mind, the-tender-heart) appears with an empty `alt` in this component, while the exact same files carry full descriptive alt text on `/shop/`, `/`, and their own product pages. Line 50 (the small 64px "chosen" preview circles) is also `alt=""`, which is more defensible since those are pure UI-state confirmation, not content images.
- **Why it matters:** same root issue as #1 — a component-wide bug, not a one-off, and it undermines the file-level alt-text signal Google would otherwise associate with these images from their other, correctly-labeled appearances.
- **Fix:** in `StackBuilder.tsx:38`, pass the product name through (the component already has `p` in scope with product data) — e.g. `alt={p.name}` or `` alt={`${p.name} bracelet`} ``.

#### 3. (Medium) No responsive images anywhere — one fixed-resolution JPEG serves every display context
- **Evidence:** no `srcset`/`sizes` attribute exists on any of the 189 `<img>` tags checked, and `next/image` optimization is fully disabled site-wide (`images: { unoptimized: true }` in `apps/web/next.config.*`, required by the static-export/GitHub-Pages architecture). Concretely: `products/the-anchor/main.jpg` is a single 1200×1200 JPEG (119 KB) that is reused — unresized — as: a ~360px-wide grid tile on `/shop/` and `/` (4-column grid inside a 96rem/`container-x` max-width), the full detail-page image on `/products/the-anchor/`, and a 64px-wide "chosen" circle inside `StackBuilder.tsx` and a 64–80px cart-line thumbnail. At the small end this is roughly 9–19× more pixels than the display box needs even at 2× device pixel ratio; conversely, the hero photos (`hero-1.jpg` 2000×1125, `hero-2.jpg` 1280×1125) are full-bleed section backgrounds that can exceed their own native resolution on wide desktop monitors, so the same "one size" approach simultaneously over-serves small contexts and under-serves the largest one.
- **Why it matters:** on UAE mobile connections, shoppers on the 2-column mobile grid or the cart drawer pay full 1200px-JPEG bandwidth for images displayed at a fraction of that size — pure waste that slows down exactly the pages closest to checkout.
- **Fix:** pre-generate 2–3 width variants per source image at build time (e.g. a `scripts/resize-images.mjs` using `sharp`, run in CI before `next build`, output alongside the originals as `main-400.jpg`/`main-800.jpg`/`main-1200.jpg`) and add `srcset`/`sizes` to the shared `Img` component. This is compatible with `images.unoptimized: true` — you're pre-baking the resize step yourself instead of asking Next to do it at request time, which is exactly what unoptimized static export requires.

#### 4. (Medium) 100% JPEG, 0% WebP/AVIF — real savings left on the table
- **Evidence:** all 34 unique images returned `content-type: image/jpeg` on live fetch; no `<picture>` element or format negotiation exists anywhere in the markup. Total unique-image payload is 6.36 MB; the single largest file is the home hero at 543.5 KB (2000×1125) — above the skill's 300 KB "warning" line and approaching the 700 KB "critical" line for a hero/banner image. Several intention/stack photos sit at 210–370 KB functioning as **content** images (not heroes), which is above that tier's 200 KB target.
- **Why it matters:** WebP/AVIF typically cut JPEG payload 25–35% at equivalent visual quality with no server-side conversion needed — this is a build-time re-encode, fully compatible with `images.unoptimized: true` (the constraint that's blocked is Next's *automatic runtime* optimization, not pre-converting the source files yourself).
- **Fix:** add a `cwebp -q 82` (or `sharp .webp()`) pass to the same build-time resize script from Finding #3, output `.webp` alongside the `.jpg`, and wrap the shared `Img` component's output in a `<picture>` with a WebP `<source>` and the existing JPEG as the `<img>` fallback. Estimated result: hero-1.jpg ~543 KB → ~350–380 KB; home-page total image weight (4.42 MB across all `<img>` refs) down roughly 25–30%.

#### 5. (Medium) Zero of the 34 AI-generated images carry the IPTC `DigitalSourceType` label
- **Evidence:** searched all 34 downloaded files for XMP packets, Photoshop/IPTC-IIM APP13 segments, and the literal strings `DigitalSourceType` / `trainedAlgorithmicMedia` — only one file (`intentions/love.jpg`) contains any IPTC-IIM segment at all, and even that one does not contain a `DigitalSourceType` field. `README.md`/`PLATFORM.md` confirm all product and lifestyle photography is AI-generated (Higgsfield, 2026-09-03), and this task's own instructions confirm the same.
- **Why it matters:** this is **not** a general ranking factor, but Google Merchant Center's AI-generated-content policy requires `IPTC DigitalSourceType: TrainedAlgorithmicMedia` on AI-generated product imagery — feeds missing this label can be disapproved. Crystal Basket's Shopify back office (ADR 0002) makes it plausible this catalog gets fed into a Google & YouTube / Merchant Center sales channel at some point; if that happens with these exact image files, the feed is at risk of rejection on the AI-image policy alone.
- **Fix:** before (or as part of) any Merchant Center / Google Shopping channel setup, batch-inject the label into the 12 product `main.jpg`/`lifestyle.jpg` files (and arguably the lifestyle/intention/stack photos too, since they're equally AI-generated) with `exiftool -XMP-iptcExt:DigitalSourceType="https://cv.iptc.org/newscodes/digitalsourcetype/trainedAlgorithmicMedia" <file>`, or the skill's own `iptc_ai_label.py inject <path> --source-type trainedAlgorithmicMedia` once `exiftool` is available in the build/deploy environment (not installed on this machine — `brew`/`exiftool` are both absent, so this has to run somewhere else, e.g. a one-off local machine with Homebrew, or a CI step with `apt-get install libimage-exiftool-perl`). This does not require touching page markup, only the binary image assets in `apps/web/public/images/`.

#### 6. (Low) No explicit `width`/`height` HTML attributes anywhere (CLS risk is present in principle, low in practice)
- **Evidence:** grep of the raw HTML confirms zero `<img>` tags carry `width=`/`height=` anywhere on the site (`grep -o '<img[^>]*>' raw/pages/*.html` — 100% missing across all 189 instances). In every case checked, the image sits inside a Tailwind `aspect-*` utility wrapper or a fixed-height hero section, which reserves layout space via CSS before the image decodes.
- **Why it matters:** this technically violates the CLS-prevention checklist, but because CSS already reserves the box in every instance sampled, real-world CLS impact is low — this is a defense-in-depth gap, not an active layout-shift bug. It matters more if CSS ever fails to load in time (e.g. a slow connection where the render-blocking stylesheet is delayed) or if a future component is added without the aspect-ratio wrapper convention.
- **Fix:** low priority — pass `width`/`height` matching each image's native pixel dimensions into the shared `Img` component alongside the resize-pipeline work in Finding #3 (you'll already be computing per-variant dimensions at that point, so this is nearly free to add at the same time).
